INtime Coder – your real-time application, from one form

How it works. Below, you describe your real-time application – what it does and what device it talks to, in your own words. A bench with real INtime nodes generates the solution, builds it, runs it for two minutes against a simulated device, measures it and films the screens. You get an e-mail with one ZIP: the solution for Visual Studio 2019 and 2022, and the recording of it running. No INtime licence is needed to try it.

What does your software connect to?
Tick the one that applies – Ethernet or a card, not both. Whatever you tick, the far end is played by a simulator: a Python window on Windows, standing where your device would stand, on the same private wire, at the same address and port. Tick nothing and we take it that nothing is connected.
What you get back A ZIP: the solution for Visual Studio 2019 and 2022, and a recording of the screens of the computer that ran it.
  • Your solution, built for Visual Studio 2019 and for Visual Studio 2022 – for the case that you have an INtime development environment on your PC.
  • A recording of the screens of the computer that ran your application – a measured run, for the case that you have no INtime environment.
  • Real I/O protocols simulated end to end – not a toy loop, built according to what you specify.
  • Want an INtime environment of your own? Please press for registering to get INtime evaluation software and one month license
  • Nothing is installed on your side for the demonstration itself – it runs on our bench.
Answer the question above and the interview opens.

What does it speak?
CAN · ARINC-429 · MIL-STD-1553 · RS-232 / RS-422 / RS-485 · analog in or out · digital lines · counters, encoders and pulse timing · something else on a card
We will use UDP.

TCP retransmits and coalesces, and those delays belong to the network stack – not to INtime. They would land in the very histogram you are here to look at. UDP sends when it is told to, so what you see is the RTOS.

Then we will use TCP – and the delivery will say plainly which part of the spread is TCP’s rather than INtime’s.

Who this request belongs to

Filled once. It is remembered in this browser, so the next request starts where this one left off, and it travels with the request so our reply comes back to the right project.
